sow.alignment: Second Week 3 exemplar: core Foundation-relevant genome modification (4.10) and initial evaluation (4.14). The Bt example also supports Biology-specific 4.12B. Prepares for C31 “Evaluate GM (research & digital slideshow; links RE).” It does not replace Week 4 independent research/slideshow. Enzyme/vector detail is optional Higher-tier stretch (4.11), never a core success gate.

safety: Paper and screen lesson; no live organisms, biological cultures or chemical work.
practicalAlternative: All evidence is supplied for offline use. Discuss, point, annotate or dictate instead of cutting cards or writing extended prose.

access.supported: Same scientific objective, with chunked cards, word bank, read-aloud access and short evidence stems. Accept accurately explained oral or annotated responses.
access.standard: Use two evidence sources and a reasoned explanation independently.
access.stretch: Evaluate limitations, explain a mechanism and transfer to unfamiliar evidence.
access.regulation: Offer solo or partner working and a quiet response route. Preview the sequence; allow a brief reset and re-entry at the next numbered task. No compulsory performance or timed competition.

title: Genetic engineering: change, test, decide
subtitle: Explain the mechanism and make a provisional crop-trial recommendation
objective: Describe genetic engineering and use evidence to weigh a specific benefit, a risk and an unanswered question.
priorLearning: A gene is a DNA section that can carry instructions affecting proteins/characteristics.
Selective breeding chooses which organisms reproduce across generations.
Natural selection can make inherited resistance more common in a population.
success: Describe genetic engineering as a direct alteration of an organism’s DNA/genome.
Connect a genetic change to a useful product or trait without claiming a change of species.
Give an evidence-based provisional decision with one benefit, one risk and one further check.

vocabulary.meaning: An organism’s complete set of genetic information.
Using laboratory technologies to directly alter an organism’s DNA.
Using genetic information to make a functional product, such as a protein.
An organism whose genetic information has been altered using genetic engineering.
Bacillus thuringiensis, a bacterium from which some pest-control protein genes originate.
A conclusion supported now, which can change when new evidence is added.

equipment: Shared trial brief and selected response page; pen or mini-whiteboard.
Offline HTML/PPTX; calculator optional for stretch comparison.
preparation: Explain that the crop trial is a constructed sample, not a claim about a named product or UK approval.
Print the evidence page; no online reading is needed for this lesson.
Keep mechanism teaching brief and concrete. Optional enzyme detail is for pupils ready for Higher-tier material, outside the Foundation core gate.

misconceptions.claim: All genetic engineering means moving a gene between species.
misconceptions.correction: It can add, change or delete DNA; some methods do not add another species’ DNA.
misconceptions.check: Ask pupils to give two kinds of DNA change.

misconceptions.claim: A bacterium given an insulin gene becomes human.
misconceptions.correction: It remains a bacterium but can produce the coded protein under suitable conditions.
misconceptions.check: Ask what is recovered and purified: the protein or a human organism?

misconceptions.claim: Every GM crop has the same benefits and risks.
misconceptions.correction: Assess the particular trait, crop, environment and evidence.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether target-insect damage data measure food safety or effects on every species.

misconceptions.claim: Pests become resistant because they need to.
misconceptions.correction: Inherited variants differ in survival and reproduction; resistance can spread across generations.
misconceptions.check: Ask what existed before exposure and what changed in later generations.

slides.title: A crop makes a pest-control protein
body: What changed: the DNA, the whole species, or the weather?
Today: explain the change and assess a trial.
slides.notes: Take a prediction and preserve it for review. Say that genetic engineering describes a method; evidence must be about a specific application. Announce the independent product: a short trial recommendation for a grower, not a blanket vote on all GM organisms.

slides.title: Retrieve genes and selection
body: R1. What is a gene?
R2. What do humans choose in selective breeding?
R3. Can a resistance trait become more common over generations?
slides.notes: R1 a section of DNA with genetic information; many genes code for proteins. R2 which organisms reproduce, selecting for desired inherited characteristics. R3 yes, through differential survival/reproduction of inherited variants. Accept plain language then model the scientific term. No disclosure of personal medical or family information.

slides.title: What genetic engineering means
body: Laboratory technologies alter the genome directly.
DNA may be added, changed or removed.
A gene transfer is one example, not the only method.
slides.notes: Think aloud: 'Selective breeding chooses parents. Genetic engineering directly changes genetic information using laboratory technology. Both can alter characteristics, but the method differs.' Do not imply every DNA change alters phenotype or every engineered organism includes a foreign gene. The drawing uses symbolic segments, not real base sequences.

visual.title: Engineering changes DNA directly
visual.description: Three conceptual changes to a DNA sequence: adding a DNA segment, changing bases, or deleting a segment. Different methods perform these changes. Diagrams are symbolic blocks, not actual DNA sequences or laboratory protocols.

elements.text: A genome is all an organism’s genetic information.
Cross-species transfer is only one method.

slides.title: Connect the change to the trait
body: A gene can affect the protein a cell makes.
A Bt crop can make a protein harmful to certain insect pests.
Testing checks whether the intended effect occurs.
slides.notes: Point across DNA → protein → possible trait. Say: 'This gene carries information used to make a protein. The protein has a biological effect on certain target pests. I should not say the plant becomes a bacterium or kills every insect.' Use only a simplified model; expression depends on the cell and appropriate control information.

visual.title: A DNA change can alter a characteristic
visual.description: Conceptual gene expression chain: a changed or added functional gene can alter the protein made and therefore a characteristic. It may need appropriate control sequences and cellular conditions; not every DNA change changes phenotype.

elements.text: Connect a genetic change to its effect

A Bt gene can enable a crop to make a protein
that harms certain insect pests.
Simplified model; the change must be checked.

slides.title: The product is the protein
body: Engineered microbial cells can make human insulin.
The product is recovered, purified and checked.
The cells do not become human.
slides.notes: Model the distinction: 'A useful instruction has changed what the cell can produce; it has not supplied a complete human genome. The medicine is a checked protein product.' This is a biological application, not medical guidance. Do not ask who uses insulin or why. Detailed manufacturing steps are outside this lesson.

visual.title: A useful protein, not a change of species
visual.description: Conceptual recombinant insulin production: genetic instructions for human insulin are introduced into suitable microbial cells, which produce protein. The insulin is recovered, purified and checked; patients receive medicine, not the engineered organisms. No laboratory protocol is supplied.

elements.text:
Recover, purify
and check
the medicine

The cells remain microbes.
The gene is information.
Insulin is the product.
Conceptual model, not a practical method.

slides.title: Predict a risk using biology
body: Pest populations contain inherited variation.
Resistant survivors can reproduce.
Resistance may spread, so monitor it.
slides.notes: Shares the preceding 3-minute I do stage. Briefly connect to natural selection: the pesticide protein does not teach insects to resist. Variants that already arise can be selected. Integrated pest-management and refuge strategies can delay resistance but are not a guarantee. This is a mechanism diagram, not observed data.

visual.title: The crop and the pest can both change
visual.description: A conceptual resistance mechanism across pest generations. The crop kills susceptible pests; rare inherited resistance variants can survive and reproduce, making resistance more common. The diagram shows a mechanism, not numerical data.

elements.text:
Pests vary.
Some inherited
variants resist
the Bt protein.

Susceptible
pests are killed.
Resistant pests
may survive.

Survivors
reproduce.

Monitoring and resistance-management strategies
can delay resistance, but not promise zero risk.

slides.title: Trial board: what does the evidence show?
body: W1. Compare damage and yield in this trial.
W2. Which claim is justified: promise, success here, or proof everywhere?
Use exact quantities.
slides.notes: Spend 2 minutes reading the table, 2 minutes group/solo evidence verdict and 3 minutes additional-question selection on next slide. Constructed data show22 fewer damaged plants per100 and1.0 t/ha greater mean yield. A provisional benefit at this site/season is supported. The table does not show the need for fewer sprays, food safety, effects on other species or long-term outcomes. Both groups received no target-insect spray.

table.caption: Constructed sample data: means from three matched plot pairs at one site in one season; neither crop received target-insect spray. Other growing conditions matched.

slides.title: Spend your two next checks
body: W3. Choose two: repeat sites/seasons; monitor resistance; measure crop colour; count likes online.
Defend how each choice reduces uncertainty.
Acknowledge a further question your choices leave open.
slides.notes: Shares 7-minute We do. Best choices from these four are repeat sites/seasons and resistance monitoring: they address generalisation and loss of efficacy. Crop colour does not answer the stated damage/yield/resistance question unless a new relevant mechanism is proposed; online popularity is not biological evidence. Other real evidence, including non-target effects and crop-specific safety assessment, remains necessary. Pupils can point to two choices and explain quietly.

slides.title: Which explanation is scientifically sound?
body: Choose the statement you would keep in a textbook.
slides.notes: Private response before feedback. Reteach A/D by revisiting the three types of DNA change; B by distinguishing gene information from whole-organism identity. C is the secure core definition.

options.text: Engineering always transfers DNA between species.
options.feedback: Adding another species’ DNA is one method; DNA may also be changed or deleted.
It remains a bacterium; it can make a useful protein.

options.text: Engineering alters DNA and may introduce a useful characteristic.
options.feedback: This describes the method without promising that every change works.

options.text: Engineering guarantees that all offspring are safer.
options.feedback: No blanket guarantee follows from the method; the actual organism and application require evidence.

slides.title: Write a provisional recommendation
body: Use the mechanism and crop-trial evidence.
Recommend a next step with a benefit, risk and missing check.
Choose your response route with the teacher.
slides.notes: Independent product: a grower should understand what has been engineered, what this evidence supports and what remains to investigate. Choose Supported/Standard/Stretch, not all three. At minute4 ask pupils to separate a measured benefit from a predicted risk; at minute8 check their next step is specific.

slides.title: A recommendation is more than a vote
body: In this trial, … so a possible benefit is …
However, … could happen because …
I recommend … while checking …
slides.notes: Shares 11-minute independent stage. Reasoned recommendations can differ. Strong evidence supports continuing carefully controlled testing; simply asserting all GM is good/bad is insufficient. A supported oral response can meet all core success criteria.

slides.title: Optional Higher-tier extension
body: Ready for more? Use the extra mechanism box on the Stretch page.
Explain a vector, restriction enzyme and ligase.
This detail is not needed for today’s core success.
slides.notes: Shares independent stage; do not teach this to all pupils or use it as a Foundation gate. The Stretch page supplies a conceptual explanation of a classical recombinant-DNA method including complementary sticky ends, not a lab protocol. Other engineering methods exist.

slides.title: Review a recommendation fairly
body: Does it explain the genetic change?
Does it separate evidence from uncertainty?
Use one audience question to sharpen the next step.
slides.notes: Light Lundy loop: pupils choose written/oral/annotated response and an audience; the teacher responds to one practical suggested check and records a class next question for Week4. Avoid framing a pupil’s preference as a scientific fact.

slides.title: Carry a good question into Week 4
body: Which crop and trait are being assessed?
What evidence would answer our unanswered question?
Who would be affected by the decision?
slides.notes: Shares the3-minute review. This is a bridge to the SoW Week4 research/digital-slideshow evaluation, not its replacement. Record a question pupils can later research using checked sources, such as effectiveness in another climate or effects on non-target organisms.

slides.title: Explain, support, qualify
body: E1. Define genetic engineering in one sentence.
E2. Give one measured benefit in the trial.
E3. Give one risk and a useful next check.
slides.notes: E1 direct alteration of DNA/genome by laboratory technology. E2 fewer damaged plants30→8 per100 or higher mean yield6.9→7.9 t/ha in this constructed trial. E3 resistance may spread; monitor resistant pests/efficacy over generations. Accept other specific plausible risks paired with relevant tests, not ungrounded certainty.

pupilPages.title: Shared evidence | Bt crop trial board
pupilPages.intro: This is a paper evaluation. Crop-trial numbers are constructed sample data, not observations from a named commercial product.

cards.title: Mechanism
cards.text: Some Bt crops contain added genetic information originating from Bacillus thuringiensis. The crop can produce a protein that harms particular insect pests. It does not become a bacterium and is not protected from every pest.

cards.title: Possible resistance risk
cards.text: Pests vary. Inherited variants that survive exposure may reproduce, so resistance can become more common over generations. Monitoring and resistance-management strategies aim to delay this.

cards.title: Evidence limits
cards.text: The trial covers one site and one season. It reports damage and yield, not food safety or effects on every non-target species. Neither crop received target-insect spray. All applications need evidence relevant to the crop, trait and setting.

blocks.text: Constructed sample data: means from three matched plot pairs. Water, fertiliser and planting density were matched. One site; one season.

blocks.prompt: W1–W2. What does the trial show, and which claim goes beyond it?
W3. Choose two next checks: repeat sites/seasons; monitor resistance; measure crop colour; count likes online. Justify them.

pupilPages.title: Supported route | Build your recommendation
pupilPages.intro: Use the shared evidence. You may speak, annotate or dictate. Words: DNA • protein • target pest • evidence • resistance • test.

blocks.prompt: S1. Finish: genetic engineering directly alters … . A Bt gene can help the crop make … .
S2. Choose one trial comparison. Include both numbers and what they measure.
S3. Explain one benefit for this crop in this trial. Do not say it proves all GM organisms are the same.
S4. Finish: resistance may become more common because surviving pests … .
S5. Recommend a next step. Name one question and a test that could answer it.

pupilPages.title: Standard route | Evidence-based trial recommendation
pupilPages.intro: Write for a grower who needs a clear reasoned next step, not a slogan.

blocks.prompt: M1. Explain how genetic engineering differs from selective breeding. Include the direct DNA change.
M2. Explain how an added Bt gene can change crop performance. Connect DNA, protein and a target-pest effect.
M3. Compare damage and yield using the constructed trial values. Identify one benefit that is supported here.
M4. Explain a plausible risk using a biological mechanism. Identify one question the table does not answer.
M5. Give your provisional recommendation and a specific next test. Explain what result might change your view.

pupilPages.title: Stretch route | Evaluate and extend
pupilPages.intro: Choose T1–T3 for deeper evaluation. T4 is an optional Higher-tier mechanism extension; it is not required for the Foundation core.

blocks.text: Constructed sample data: original trial mean yield non-GM6.9 versus Bt7.9 t/ha; target-pest damage30 versus8 plants per100. A second season at another site gives non-GM7.1 versus Bt7.0 t/ha and damage5 versus4 plants per100. Different pest pressure and growing conditions may matter.

blocks.prompt: T1. Compare both yield differences and damage differences. What does the second setting change about your conclusion?
T2. Explain why neither trial alone establishes food safety or all environmental effects. Propose one focused additional investigation.
T3. State a provisional recommendation that considers a benefit, a risk, a missing piece of evidence and who might be affected.

blocks.text: Optional Higher-tier mechanism box: in one classical method, a restriction enzyme cuts DNA at particular sequences. Compatible short single-stranded ends (“sticky ends”) can pair. Ligase joins the DNA backbone. A vector, such as a plasmid, carries the DNA into a suitable cell. This is one conceptual method, not all genetic engineering.

blocks.prompt: T4. Explain the different jobs of the restriction enzyme, complementary sticky ends, ligase and vector. Why does inserting DNA not guarantee a useful product?

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection | A precise judgement
pupilPages.intro: Answer independently. A short oral or annotated answer is valid.

blocks.prompt: E1. Define genetic engineering in one sentence.
E2. Give one measured benefit from the constructed trial: non-GM damage30/100 and yield6.9 t/ha; Bt damage8/100 and yield7.9 t/ha.
E3. Give one plausible risk and a useful next check.
L1. What audience question sharpened your recommendation?
L2. Write one question to take into the Week4 GM research and digital slideshow.
My next useful step is…
choices: Read a comparison with its units.
Match an uncertainty to a test.

answers.label: R1–R3 retrieval
answers.answer: R1 a gene is a section of DNA containing genetic information; many code for proteins. R2 humans choose which organisms reproduce for desired inherited traits. R3 yes: inherited variants that survive and reproduce can become more common in later generations.

answers.label: W1 / S2 / M3 data comparisons
answers.answer: Constructed trial: damage falls from30 to8 plants per100, a difference of22 plants per100 (22 percentage points if expressed as percentages). Mean yield rises from6.9 to7.9 t/ha, a difference of1.0 t/ha. These are means in one site/season, not universal outcomes. Optional relative damage reduction22/30×100≈73%; do not confuse this with22 percentage points.

answers.label: W2 justified claim / S3 benefit
answers.answer: “This trial shows a promising benefit here” is supported: less target-pest damage and higher mean yield. “Success everywhere” or “proof that all GM crops are safe” is not. Neither group received target-insect spray, so this table does not directly measure a reduction in spraying. Future reduced spray use is a possible benefit requiring its own comparison.

answers.label: W3 next checks
answers.answer: Repeat across sites/seasons tests whether the result generalises; monitor resistance tests whether pest susceptibility/effectiveness changes across generations. Crop colour is not relevant to the stated performance question without a further mechanism. Online likes measure popularity, not biological outcomes. These two checks still leave questions such as non-target effects and crop-specific safety assessment.

answers.label: S1 / E1 definition
answers.answer: Genetic engineering directly alters an organism’s DNA/genome using laboratory technology. A Bt gene can enable the crop to make a protein that harms particular insect pests. DNA may be added, changed or deleted; not all engineering transfers DNA between species.

answers.label: S4 resistance mechanism
answers.answer: Pests contain inherited variation; those resistant to the protein may survive exposure and reproduce, passing on relevant alleles. Resistance can therefore become more common across generations. Do not accept that individual pests intentionally change because they need to survive.

answers.label: S5 / M5 provisional recommendation
answers.answer: Model: continue controlled trials with resistance monitoring before making a wider-use recommendation. The initial reduction in damage is promising, but test matched crop groups over more sites/seasons and monitor pest survival/trait effectiveness. A consistent lack of yield benefit or increasing resistance would weaken the recommendation. Accept a reasoned alternative if it uses supplied evidence and states uncertainty.

answers.label: M1 distinction
answers.answer: Selective breeding chooses parents with desired inherited traits, then breeds and selects across generations. Genetic engineering directly changes DNA using laboratory technologies. Both can influence inherited characteristics; the method distinguishes them.

answers.label: M2 mechanism
answers.answer: The added gene provides information for production of a protein in suitable plant cells. That protein affects particular target pests and may reduce damage. The crop remains a plant; not every insect is affected, and the intended trait needs testing.

answers.label: M4 risk and unknown
answers.answer: Risk: selection can increase inherited pest resistance, reducing future effectiveness. Unknowns: effects across settings, non-target species, food safety, long-term performance or social/economic consequences. Match the claim to what the table actually measures. Do not treat an unanswered question as proof of harm.

answers.label: T1 two settings
answers.answer: First yield difference Bt−non-GM=+1.0 t/ha; second=−0.1 t/ha. First damage difference=22 fewer plants per100; second=1 fewer. The second setting weakens a blanket benefit claim and suggests context (including pest pressure) matters. It does not prove the first result false or that the crop is always ineffective; means, spread and trial replication matter.

answers.label: T2 scope and investigation
answers.answer: The trials measure target-pest damage and yield, not composition/toxicity/allergenicity or every ecological interaction. A focused environmental investigation might compare abundance/survival of specified non-target organisms in matched replicated plots over time. A relevant crop-specific safety assessment would need different evidence. Do not infer safety/harm from yield alone.

answers.label: T3 balanced evaluation
answers.answer: A defensible answer links the initial benefit to reduced target-pest damage, identifies resistance or a relevant possible environmental issue, notes missing repeated/appropriate evidence, and considers growers, consumers or ecosystems. A provisional decision must be conditional, not a universal judgement on the technique.

answers.label: T4 optional Higher mechanism
answers.answer: Restriction enzyme cuts at a particular recognition sequence; complementary sticky ends can base-pair; ligase seals/joins the DNA backbone; a vector such as a plasmid carries DNA into suitable cells. Successful insertion alone does not guarantee expression, sufficient functional protein or the desired whole-organism effect, so suitable control information/conditions and checks are needed. This detail is optional Higher-tier content, not a Foundation assessment requirement.

answers.label: Hinge A–D
answers.answer: C is correct. A wrongly says all methods transfer between species. B confuses one useful gene with complete organism identity. D makes an unsupported universal safety/offspring guarantee.

answers.label: E2–E3 exit
answers.answer: E2 accept lower damage30→8 per100 or greater mean yield6.9→7.9 t/ha, explicitly in the constructed trial. E3 accept resistance with monitoring across pest generations; accept another scientifically plausible specific risk with an appropriate focused test, not a blanket assertion.

answers.label: L1–L2 reflection and Week4 bridge
answers.answer: Accept a concrete revision prompted by a question, such as naming the crop/trait, correcting a unit or identifying a missing comparison. Good Week4 questions are narrow and answerable, for example “How does this Bt trait affect a named non-target insect in a particular environment?” or “When does lower pest damage lead to a worthwhile yield gain?”

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening2, retrieval3, I do10, We do7, hinge3, independent11, review3, exit1. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.

Foundation core: genome modification, DNA/protein/trait reasoning and evidence-based evaluation. The optional Higher-tier box maps to detailed enzyme/ligase/sticky-end/vector content; do not gate the core outcome on it.

Week4 research and digital-slideshow work remains a separate SoW requirement. Carry forward pupils’ questions; use sources checked for the particular application and distinguish evidence from value judgements.
All crop numbers are constructed sample data. The cells, proteins and selection diagrams are conceptual models, not practical instructions or exact molecular drawings.

Teacher model recommendation: “The first trial suggests less target-pest damage and higher yield at this site. I would continue controlled testing with resistance monitoring because a one-season result cannot establish long-term or wider outcomes.”

Assess success through an accurate definition, a causal link from genetic information to trait/product, one numerical evidence comparison and a justified next check. Oral and annotated work can meet the same standard.

If pupils infer all GM is good/bad, ask “Which organism, which change, which measurement?” If they confuse cells with insulin, point separately to producer and purified product. If they omit uncertainty, ask which table column could answer their claim.
No pupil medical or family disclosure is requested. Insulin is used only as an example of a protein product made through biotechnology; this lesson offers no advice on diagnosis or treatment.
